_comment: Mutation testing for the reports engine: the registry that decides which report templates exist, the routes that serve and download them, the download serializers, the shared orphan-account definition, and the one built-in template. Scoped like the auth, effective-access and account-linking configs -- these files plus their own unit tests, which are self-contained (no filesystem outside the sandbox, no PostgreSQL) so they run clean inside Stryker's sandbox. WHY THESE FILES: the epic's Key Result is that adding a third report costs only a template, and that claim rests entirely on this code being generic. Both failure directions are silent: a registry that accepts a malformed template, or a route that quietly serves the wrong metadata, produces a page that renders -- just not the report anyone asked for. The orphan anti-join is the same shape of risk: too wide and every linked account is reported as orphaned, too narrow and a genuinely unattached account is invisible. Neither throws. The download serializers (export.js) fail the same silent way: a missed quote shifts every following CSV column, a dropped row is just a shorter file, and an unescaped leading `=` is a formula the user's spreadsheet executes -- the file still opens. MUTATOR SET: StringLiteral and ObjectLiteral disabled, matching the sibling API configs. Same cost, restated: the SQL in orphanQuery.js stops being mutated, so this cannot tell you the query is correct -- that stays contract-tests/reports.contract.test.js's job. THE ONE SURVIVOR IS AN ARTIFACT, NOT AN UNTESTED BRANCH: registry.js:15 builds its Map from BUILT_IN_REPORTS at module load, and Stryker's switch is not active during that first import, so `BUILT_IN_REPORTS.map(() => undefined)` can never be observed by a test in this runner. (The same artifact previously hid three real mutants behind a module-level seeding loop; the loop was removed and its validation moved into registry.test.js, which is what took this run from 94.8% to 98.3%.) Enforced: see MUTATION FLOOR below. Run: cd app/api && npm run test:mutation:reports MUTATION FLOOR: `break` is set a few points under the measured score, and is a RATCHET -- it only ever goes up. It is enforced by the weekly .github/workflows/js-mutation.yml (never on a PR: mutation is far heavier than the unit suite). The margin is not slack to spend, it absorbs the two things that legitimately move a score without anyone editing a test: a Stryker/vitest upgrade that changes which mutants are generated, and timeouts, which count as killed and can flip under CI load. Raise the floor when the score rises; never lower it to make a red run green -- a drop means a test stopped discriminating. Measured 99.15% when the floor was set to 97. RE-BASELINED TO 85 (Nov 2026, #1548), the one deliberate exception to 'never lower it': the 97 came from those first nine files, and the scope grew to 75 files (see SCOPE HISTORY at the end) with no run checking the floor, because the weekly workflow did not list this scope. After the nlreports split it holds 50 files, and their first real run scored 87.20% (3,200 killed, 403 survived, 67 uncovered). The gaps are concentrated in lib/httpJson.js (no test in the include list reaches it), application-access-review.js, export.js, unit-members.js and appRiskRules.js. 85 is that measurement minus 2, by the same rule as every other floor here, and from now on it only goes up: raise it as those files get tests (tracked in #1552). IN THE WEEKLY MATRIX since the workflow started deriving its scopes from these configs (.github/scripts/mutation_scopes.sh), so the floor above is enforced weekly. SCOPE HISTORY (which files joined this scope after it was created, why, and which are NOT YET MEASURED here -- check before relying on the floor): docs/contributing/mutation-scope-history.md#api-reports.
tests_comment: Explicit file list rather than a directory glob, same reason as the sibling stryker vitest
configs: Stryker copies app/api into a temp sandbox, so a test that reads the real
filesystem outside it resolves a path that does not exist there, fails the dry run, and
aborts the whole run before a single mutant is evaluated. Two tests of the reports code
do exactly that and are therefore left out — reportNames.guard.test.js (it scans app/ui
as well as app/api) and the contract tests (they need a PostgreSQL container).
Listed instead of excluded: an excluded test that happened to be some mutant's only
killer would surface as a false survivor, which is worse than measuring less. Every test
here is a real killer for the five mutated files.

mutationExclusions.src/reports/xlsxMatrix.js: Writes a matrix tab with ExcelJS: layout and styling around a loop. teamRoleMatrix.test.js reads the workbook back and pins the tab order and every cell. Not yet measured: Stryker gives no usable score on the Windows box this was written on.
mutationExclusions.src/reports/teamRoleMatrix.js: The unit report tab built on contexts/teamOverview.js. teamRoleMatrix.test.js pins each mark, the cap boundary, former members and the failure path. Not yet measured: Stryker gives no usable score on the Windows box this was written on.
mutationExclusions.src/contexts/assignmentCounts.js: Three SQL statements and a short wrapper that runs them in one transaction. The statements are strings, and StringLiteral mutation is off in every config here, so Stryker has almost nothing to mutate; the decisions that matter are inside those strings (what is de-duplicated, what is excluded, which rows are written) and no unit test can observe them through a SQL-blind mock. They are proven where the statements actually run: contract-tests/contextAssignmentCounts.contract.test.js, against real PostgreSQL, with every expected number distinct. The wrapper's own branches (the order, the one transaction, the row count from pg or from the embedded database, a failure passing through) are pinned by assignmentCounts.test.js.
mutationExclusions.src/reports/types.js: Contains no executable code at all: the file is the JSDoc ReportTemplate contract plus a bare `export {}`, so Stryker has nothing behavioural to mutate. Its correctness is enforced by the code that implements the contract (registry.js validates the required fields, the route projects the metadata), not by anything in this file.
mutationExclusions.src/reports/templates/index.js: Declaration only: one import per built-in template and the array that holds them — this IS the single registration line the reports seam is built around. The one mutant Stryker can make (empty the array) is killed by every registry and route test, so a run here measures the registration list rather than any logic. Behaviour lives in registry.js, which is mutated.
mutationExclusions.src/lookups/types.js: Contains no executable code at all: the file is the JSDoc LookupSource contract plus a bare `export {}`. Same shape and same reason as src/reports/types.js — the contract is enforced by registry.js, which validates the required fields and IS mutated.
mutationExclusions.src/lookups/sources/index.js: Declaration only: one import per built-in lookup source and the array that holds them — the single registration line the lookup seam is built around. The one mutant Stryker can make (empty the array) is killed by the registry and route tests, so a run here measures the registration list rather than any logic.
mutationExclusions.src/reports/heldEntitlements.js: Entitlement Pivot on a unit of accounts: the resources its direct members hold, counted among them. Not yet measured: Stryker gives no usable score on the Windows box this was written on; covered by its unit/mount tests, to move into a mutate list once measured in CI.
